claim: The continuity hypothesis: dreams reflect waking-life experiences, and the more time spent on an activity, the more it tends to appear in dreams.
citation: Schredl (2003), continuity hypothesis; summarised in Lambrecht, Schredl, Henley-Einion & Blagrove (2013), International Journal of Dream Research 6(1)
confidence: Well replicated for thematic continuity; mechanisms debated

claim: In an online study of 1,966 people, more consumption of each media type, and more emotional involvement with it, correlated with a higher share of dreams about that media.
citation: Moverley, Schredl & Göritz (2018), Media dreaming and media consumption: an online study, International Journal of Dream Research 11(2), 127-134

claim: Most of 1,375 UK library users said their dreams were affected by reading, TV and daily activities; the more time they spent on an activity, the more likely they reported an effect.
citation: Lambrecht, Schredl, Henley-Einion & Blagrove (2013), International Journal of Dream Research 6(1), 41-44

claim: DreamBank is a research archive of over 27,000 dream reports, used here as a rough baseline for how common each symbol is.
citation: Domhoff & Schneider (2008), Studying dream content using the archive and search engine on DreamBank.net, Consciousness and Cognition 17(4), 1238-1247
confidence: Large archive, but skewed towards a few long-term dreamers and older US samples

claim: Features of waking events tend to reappear in dreams the next day (day-residue) and again 5 to 7 days later (dream-lag), a U-shaped pattern over a week. The study found the dream-lag effect in REM dreams but not in NREM stage 2 dreams.
citation: Blagrove, Fouquet, Henley-Einion, Pace-Schott, Davies, Neuschaffer & Turnbull (2011), Assessing the dream-lag effect for REM and NREM stage 2 dreams, PLoS ONE
confidence: Moderate: lab study; effect seen for REM dreams only

claim: Dreams usually contain fragments of personal waking experiences rather than replaying a whole episode: in two-week diaries from 32 people, over 80% of dreams showed low to moderate traces of autobiographical memory, and only 1 dream (0.5%) relived an episode.
citation: Malinowski & Horton (2014), Memory sources of dreams: the incorporation of autobiographical rather than episodic experiences, Journal of Sleep Research 23(4), 441-447

claim: In the Hall and Van de Castle norms (500 dream reports each from male and female US college students), negative emotions made up 80% of all emotions reported, misfortunes appeared in about a third of dreams, and good fortunes in only 6%.
citation: Hall & Van de Castle norms for American college students, as reported by DreamResearch.net (UC Santa Cruz)
confidence: Well established, but older US student samples

claim: Dream content tends to be continuous with the dreamer's waking concerns, memories and behaviour; the Hall and Van de Castle system counts content categories as percentages so dreams of different lengths can be compared.
citation: Domhoff (2005), The dreams of men and women: patterns of gender similarity and difference, DreamResearch.net (UC Santa Cruz)
confidence: Well supported by content-analysis research; unpublished paper

claim: Evidence suggests frequent video game play may modestly increase lucid dreaming, more strongly increases control over dreams, and is linked to finding nightmares less frightening.
citation: Gackenbach (2012), Video game play and consciousness, chapter: Dreams and video game play
confidence: Emerging: mostly correlational studies of gamers

claim: The Hall and Van de Castle system codes five dream emotions: anger, apprehension (fear, anxiety, guilt, embarrassment), sadness, confusion and happiness. Emotions are scored only when the dreamer states them, or shows a clear physical reaction such as crying, and are not inferred from the setting.
citation: Hall & Van de Castle coding rules for emotions, DreamResearch.net (UC Santa Cruz)
confidence: Standard method in dream content research

claim: On DreamBank reports with Hall and Van de Castle emotion codes, an off-the-shelf sentiment model matched human scores poorly (about 52-53 F1 on positive emotions), while a supervised BERT-large model reached about 85-87 F1 and held up on dream series it had not seen.
citation: Bertolini, Elce, Michalak & Bernardi, Automatic scoring of dream reports' emotional content with large language models (arXiv preprint, 2023)
confidence: Single study; supervised model, not a prompted chatbot

claim: A tool that automatically scores dream reports on the Hall and Van de Castle scale had an average error of 0.24 against hand-annotated reports, and applied to 24,000 reports it found support for the continuity hypothesis.
citation: Fogli, Aiello & Quercia (2020), Our dreams, our selves: automatic analysis of dream reports, Royal Society Open Science
confidence: Peer-reviewed; rule-based tool rather than an LLM

claim: Some dream themes are near-universal: in a survey of 1,181 Canadian university students, 81.5% had dreamed of being chased, 73.8% of falling and 67.1% of school or studying at least once. Other themes were rare, such as being an object (3.5%). These are lifetime figures, not how often each theme appears per dream.
citation: Nielsen, Zadra, Simard, Saucier, Stenstrom, Smith & Kuiken (2003). The typical dreams of Canadian university students. Dreaming 13(4), 211-235.
confidence: Large sample; self-report of lifetime prevalence, so subject to memory bias (noted by the authors)
